html: NF-κB is held in the cytoplasm by its own inhibitor. The p65:p50 dimer is bound to IκBα, which covers the dimer's nuclear localisation signals, and what a Toll-like receptor does is remove that inhibitor. The signal passes as ubiquitin chains before any kinase is involved: TRAF6, recruited to the receptor's Myddosome, builds lysine 63-linked chains on itself with the dimeric E2 Ubc13:Uev1A, and TAB2 binds those chains and brings TAK1, which phosphorylates itself and then the activation loop of IKKβ. The IKK complex, IKKβ with IKKα and the regulatory NEMO, phosphorylates IκBα at Ser32 and Ser36, the motif that SCF-βTrCP recognises to ubiquitinate it, and the proteasome destroys IκBα while releasing the dimer intact. NF-κB then enters the nucleus within minutes. Two of the genes it switches on first are its own brakes. NFKBIA is transcribed and translated within the hour, and the new IκBα enters the nucleus, strips NF-κB from DNA and carries it back out, which returns the system to its latent state and, when the stimulus persists, makes nuclear NF-κB oscillate. TNFAIP3 encodes A20, a deubiquitinase that removes the chains from TRAF6, so the signal is ended at its source; macrophages without A20 keep TRAF6 ubiquitinated and NF-κB active long after endotoxin, and the mice die of uncontrolled inflammation. The two loops differ in what they end: IκBα resets the transcription factor, and A20 shuts down the receptor side, which is why losing A20 and not IκBα leaves the cell unable to stop responding.
